newsitem.title: UK: "Cocktail" AIDS therapy means empty hospital beds.
newsitem.headline: "Cocktail" AIDS therapy means empty hospital beds.

text.p: New "cocktail" therapies that combine drugs to reduce HIV virus levels are having dramatic results, emptying hospital beds and giving patients new hope, doctors told a conference on Monday.

They called on governments that have not approved the combination therapy for AIDS sufferers to do so quickly, saying the new approach will not only prolong lives but also save money for health services.
"We are talking about a 40 to 50 percent reduction in mortality," said Dr Ian Weller of London's Middlesex Hospital, one of the organisers of the conference.
He said the good effects had lasted up to two years in some cases. "There is a tremendous air of optimism, and rightly so."
Dr Peter Reiss of the Academy Medical Centre in Amsterdam, where a mixture of three drugs is routinely available, said his specialty AIDS clinic had started emptying out.

"What didn't happen for years happened a few months ago, where half the beds in this unit were not taken up by HIV patients," he told a news conference. Instead, they were being treated as out-patients, coming in for check-ups and medicine.
"Since we started these therapies we have seen a complete transformation," said Dr Peter Ruane, a doctor specialising in AIDS in Los Angeles.

Studies earlier this year showed a triple combination of Glaxo-Wellcome's AZT or a similar drug such as Roche's Hivid (ddC) with another such drug, plus a new class of drug known as protease inhibitor, pushed the virus down to almost undetectable levels.

Nine different AIDS drugs are now available in Europe and 10 in the United States. With better methods for measuring virus levels and the strength of the immune system, doctors now had a good armoury of weapons to fight the disease, Weller said.
Ruane said a measurable sign was a reduction in cytomegalovirus (CMV), a herpes infection that can blind AIDS patients.
"We're just not seeing any new CMV disease," Ruane told the Third International Conference on Drug Therapy in HIV Infection being held in Birmingham. "It's extraordinary."
He said a common cancer that also infects AIDS patients was disappearing. "Patients with Kaposi's sarcoma...were watching the lesions actually disappear."
Ruane said the patients were not given specific drugs for CMV or Kaposi's. Rather, their recovered immune systems seemed to be fighting off the diseases.

The first AIDS drug, AZT, proved a huge disappointment when studies showed it did not help patients live any longer over time. But combinations hit the virus at various stages of its replicative cycle and prevent the virus mutating into drug-resistant forms.

"If you hit it hard with multiple drugs you can drive it down until it is not reproducing and then it cannot become resistant," said Dr Charles Farthing of the AIDS Healthcare Foundation in Los Angeles. But Farthing said the drugs must not be misused.
"The downside is if you stop these drugs the virus comes right back." He said many cautious doctors would prescribe fewer drugs, and in low doses.
"We must persuade doctors not to be conservative -- to use the full dose up front and early in the disease."
Weller said long-term studies were not yet available because the drugs were so new. "We mustn't go over the top," he said.
